Getting Better Results

How to write requests that get useful, specific, School Tech-relevant answers - not generic ones.
For Team Members
The core idea: The fix for a weak answer is almost always more detail about your specific situation - not more background about the company. This guide shows exactly what detail to add, with School Tech examples.

The Three-Ingredient Formula
Most weak prompts are missing one of these three things. A request that includes all three almost always gets a useful first response.
1 — What
What you need
The actual task or question. Be direct - don't build up to it.
"Draft a response to this customer email" not "I'm wondering if you could maybe help me with something a customer sent"
2 — Context
The relevant situation
What the tool needs to know to be specific. Paste the actual content when you have it.
"Here is the email they sent: [paste]" or "This is for a district using our HR module, mid-year renewal"
3 — Format
What you want back
Length, tone, structure. Optional, but saves back-and-forth when you have a specific need.
"Keep it under 3 sentences" or "Use bullet points" or "Formal tone - this is for a superintendent"
You don't always need all three. A clear question with good context often doesn't need a format instruction. But if your first response is too long, too generic, or the wrong tone - that is almost always a missing Format or missing Context problem. Add one and ask again.
Before and After - School Tech Examples
These examples show the same request written two ways. The "after" version adds context and gets a more useful response without much more effort.
Example 1 - Customer response
✘ Before
Help me write a response to a customer complaint.
The tool has to guess: What did they complain about? What product? What outcome do you want?
✓ After
A customer emailed saying their time clock stopped syncing punches after last Tuesday's update. They sound frustrated - this is their second time reporting it. Draft a response that acknowledges the issue, gives them a realistic timeline (we're still diagnosing), and keeps the tone calm and professional. Here's their email: [paste]
Tool knows: the issue, the history, the tone goal, and the actual content to work from.
The "after" version takes 20 extra seconds to write and saves several rounds of back-and-forth. You will almost always get a usable first draft instead of a generic template.
Example 2 - Policy or process question
✘ Before
What's our renewal process?
Renewal for what? Which product? What stage are they at? Which district type?
✓ After
Walk me through the renewal process for a Skyward Qmlativ district that is 60 days out from contract end. They've been a customer for 4 years and always renew - I just need to know the standard steps and who owns each one.
The tool can give you the actual steps instead of a generic overview.
Product, timing, and customer situation are the three details that turn a generic process explanation into an actionable answer.
Example 3 - Troubleshooting or diagnosis
✘ Before
A customer is having issues with their time clock.
Issues how? Which clock model? Since when? What error are they seeing?
✓ After
A customer is reporting that their TT7 time clocks stopped communicating after they switched internet providers last week. The clocks show a red network light. They haven't changed any settings. What are the most likely causes and what should I ask them to check first?
Clock model, timeline, symptom, and what's already ruled out gives the tool something to work with.
For troubleshooting, the specific symptom and timeline are the most important context. A vague description gets a checklist. A specific symptom gets a diagnosis.
How to Improve a Response That Misses
The first response is a starting point, not a final product. Correcting in the same conversation is faster than starting over - the tool remembers everything said earlier in the thread.
1
Name exactly what's wrong
Don't say "that's not quite right" - say what specifically missed. The tool can fix a specific thing; it can't fix "not quite right."
"That's too formal for this customer - they're casual in their emails. Rewrite it in a friendlier tone."
2
Add the context you left out
If the response is generic, you probably left out a key detail. Add it and ask again.
"I should have mentioned - this district is a new customer, only 3 months in. The response shouldn't assume they know our process. Try again with that in mind."
3
Tell it to keep what's working
If most of a response is good but one part needs changing, say so. You don't have to throw out the whole thing.
"The first two paragraphs are good. Just rewrite the last paragraph - it sounds like we're making excuses. I want it to end on a confident, forward-looking note."
4
Ask it to show options
If you're not sure what tone or structure you want, ask for two or three versions. Pick and edit from there.
"Give me two versions of this - one short and direct, one that walks through the resolution in more detail. I'll pick which fits better."
Start a new conversation for a new topic. Within one conversation, the tool remembers everything. But if you start a new conversation, it starts fresh - it does not carry context from a previous session. For anything multi-step, stay in the same thread.
Tips by Task Type
Different kinds of requests need different context. Here is what to include for the most common use cases.
✍ Drafting communications
State the recipient and your relationship with them (new customer, frustrated customer, long-term partner, etc.)
Paste the email or message you're responding to when there is one
Say the tone goal: formal, friendly, firm, apologetic, reassuring
Say the outcome you want: schedule a call, close the ticket, set expectations, de-escalate
Try this structure: "Draft a reply to this email [paste]. The customer is [description]. I want to [outcome]. Tone: [tone]. Keep it under [length]."
🔍 Looking something up
Say what you already know - it saves the tool from repeating things you do not need
Say what decision you're trying to make - "I need this to decide whether to escalate" gets a different answer than "I'm just curious"
Name the specific product, module, or workflow you're asking about
If you are not finding what you need, ask "What else should I know about X that's relevant here?"
Try this structure: "I need to know [specific thing] about [product/process]. This is for [situation]. I already know [what you know]. What should I do?"
🔬 Troubleshooting
Give the specific symptom, not just "it's broken" - what exactly is happening?
Give the timeline - when did it start? What changed around that time?
Say what's already been ruled out or tried
Include the error message or exact wording if there is one - paste it in
Try this structure: "Customer reports [exact symptom] on [product/model] since [when]. [What changed or what they tried]. Error message: [paste if applicable]. What should we check first?"
📄 Summarizing or analyzing
Paste the full content you want summarized - do not describe it, give it
Say what you need from the summary: key decisions, action items, questions to follow up on, highlights for leadership, etc.
Say the audience for the summary - internal use vs. sharing externally vs. your own reference notes
If analyzing multiple things, give them clearly labeled (Document A / Document B, or paste with a separator)
Try this structure: "Here is [content]: [paste]. Summarize the [key points / action items / decisions] for [audience]. I need this to [purpose]."
Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
🔍
Being too vague
"Help me with this customer" or "Tell me about the renewal process" - no product, no situation, no goal.
Fix: Add the product, the customer situation, and what outcome you're working toward. Specifics cost you 10 seconds and save you 3 rounds of back-and-forth.
🗏
Describing the content instead of pasting it
"A customer sent an email complaining about billing" - the tool can do a lot more with the actual email than with your description of it.
Fix: Paste it in. Email, error message, document excerpt, log entry - paste the actual text. You can remove restricted data first (names, account numbers) and describe them with placeholders like [customer name] or [district name].
😕
Accepting a generic answer when you needed a specific one
Getting a five-step general process when you needed to know specifically what to do in your situation - and not pushing back.
Fix: Follow up with your specific situation: "That's the general process - in my case the customer is 60 days out and has a history of paying late. What specifically applies here?" The tool will narrow in.
📋
Using a response without reviewing it
Sending an AI-drafted email or process answer to a customer or colleague without checking the details first.
Fix: Treat every response as a first draft. Read it before using it. Check names, dates, product details, and any policy claims against what you know to be true. The tool is very good at structure and tone - the specific facts need your verification.
🚫
Pasting restricted data
Including customer PII, student records, employee data, or credentials when asking for help with a task.
Fix: Anonymize before pasting. Replace a customer name with "a customer" or "[customer name]". Replace a specific figure with a rounded number. You can describe the situation accurately without including the identifiable details. See the Restricted Data Reference Guide for the full list of what to leave out.
🔁
Starting over instead of iterating
Getting a response that's 80% right, abandoning it, and starting a new conversation from scratch.
Fix: Stay in the same conversation and tell it what to fix. "The structure is good but the tone is too formal - rewrite just the opening and closing paragraphs" is faster than starting over and gets a better result because the tool still has the full context.
Quick Reference - What to Say When
Situation What to add to your request
Response is too long Shorten this to 3 sentences or fewer. Keep the key point about [X].
Response is too generic That's too general. In my specific case, [situation details]. What applies here?
Tone is wrong Rewrite this in a [friendlier / more formal / more direct] tone. The recipient is [description].
Missed the point You misunderstood - the issue is not [X], it's [Y]. Try again with that in mind.
Want options to choose from Give me two versions: one [short/formal/direct] and one [longer/friendlier/detailed]. I'll pick.
Need to verify something How confident are you about [specific claim]? Is there anything I should double-check?
Not sure if the answer is complete Is there anything else relevant to this situation that I haven't asked about?
Want to improve something you wrote Here's my draft: [paste]. Improve the [clarity / tone / structure] without changing the core message.
Questions or issues? Contact Adam Baker. If a tool is consistently giving you wrong answers on a specific topic, that is feedback worth logging - it means the tool's knowledge needs updating, not that you are using it wrong.
